brief.head: A one-way door
brief.text: Amit Varma opposes the death penalty: the state is “a fumbling beast” that has executed innocent men. Ajay Shah cited a policy principle: do things that you can undo. {085-C04}

brief.head: Monkey business
brief.text: Some dictators turn out well by dumb luck, Ajay Shah said, just as some monkeys pick good portfolios. That does not make monkeys good at portfolio choice. {085-C05}

brief.head: Whiners and doers
brief.text: Asked at a party to complete “There are two kinds of people in the world”, Amit Varma said: the whiners and the doers. Pick friends who are doers. {085-C09}

brief.head: Atoms on loan
brief.text: Legacy is vanity, Amit Varma said. Ajay Shah agreed: “Life is the whim of a few trillion atoms to be you for a while.” {085-C14}

brief.head: Hold that thought
brief.text: Amit Varma judges people’s thinking by how often they interrupt. Men, he said, interrupt women on conference panels all the time, often without realising it. {085-C26}

thought.text: When you are in solitude, you have the company of yourself.

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah give the world three grades
lead.head: Rated, berated and complicated
body: The crew threw words at the hosts, and the hosts threw back one of three verdicts: underrated, overrated or complicated. Amit Varma had added the third to a familiar internet game, for things that look underrated from one angle and overrated from another. {#complicated}
The result was the show’s longest episode so far, two hours and fifteen minutes on everything from cities and cinema to Elon Musk, marriage, Maggi and death.
One word was ruled out before the first throw. Freedom, the hosts agreed, is underrated, and they speak about it so much already.

The opening verdicts came easily. Cities are underrated, Varma said, because “people are brains, not stomachs”: density brings diverse people together and lets them specialise in deeper ways. {085-C01}
Ajay Shah called villages “a hotbed of ignorance, superstition, and unfreedom”. Moving to the city, he said, “is the beginning of freedom”.
Curiosity, Shah said, is treated as something cute and juvenile. “I want to say that extended juvenility is the essence of goodness and greatness.” {085-C02}
## Agree to disagree
After the death sentence, Varma noticed a problem. “So far we are agreeing on everything. This is a bit worrying. Can we learn to disagree?” {#agreeing}

Bob Dylan obliged. Shah called him a bad singer whose songs should be left to others. Varma and the crew sang *Lay Lady Lay* in a full nasal twang, to show that some songs only Dylan can sing. {085-J03}

Then came Elon Musk. Varma called him a pioneering thinker whose bets on electric cars, batteries and space defied conventional thinking. Shah saw survivorship bias: “There are 16,384 Elon Musks. And out of dumb luck, we are venerating one.” {085-C06}

The sharpest fight was over flat-earth theory, which both called nonsense. Varma defended heretical thinking as the way humanity progresses. Shah wanted a lot less social media and a lot more reverence for knowledge. {085-C08}

They met partway, agreeing that an ordinary person can default to the conventional view while a genuine heretic should still speak up. On social media they did not: a net positive for Varma, who built his career on it, and a net negative for Shah.
## Theories of living

The middle of the episode turned personal. Varma offered his “Bengali theory” of happiness: at any moment, a small act, a song, a call to a friend, some bacon, can make the next instant happier. {085-C11}
Shah’s answer to Varma’s ode to Bengali melancholy was three words long. “Ice cream is better.” {085-J12}
They split again over pills. Varma takes modafinil on recording days, as “a tool and not a crutch”. Shah prefers no props at all, not even caffeine, because discipline builds character. {085-C21}
Even talent was marked down. What we call a child’s talent, Shah said, is usually “dumb luck and accidents”: praise for something, more practice, then skill. {085-C28}

The last word was death. Shah, worried about the longevity explosion, called it underrated. Varma said nobody really rates it at all, because everybody is in denial, and left the subject for another episode so that they could end on a happy note. {#happynote}
His philosophy of happiness, he said, is simple: “You can be happy whenever you want.”

second.label: Fathers and sons
second.head: The hug that came late
second.deck: Amit Varma on seeing parents as people, and counting the visits left
body: Amit Varma’s father, in his last years in Chandigarh, seemed to be trying to reach out. Once, as Varma was getting into his Uber after a visit, his father opened his arms. They had never really hugged. {085-S06}
Varma gave him a very awkward hug. He had once recorded his father talking about his life for a couple of hours, but it was a one-off, and a lot remained unsaid.

Most people, Varma said, see their parents only in the job description of father or mother. His exercise for readers: calculate how many more times you will see them. The number will be so small that you should call them right after the show. {#visits}

quote.text: And I went and I gave him a very awkward hug and I respected the moment. But it was just one moment.

second.caption: his father’s one awkward hug

third.head: Next stop, Kanyakumari
body: Ajay Shah is currently at about twenty trail days a year, roughly ten in the Sahyadris and ten in the Himalayas. With fewer constraints, he said, it would only be more.
His one story of hiking: he and Ayush Patnaik were walking a north-south route through the Sahyadris in Maharashtra. By day eight or nine, they looked at each other.
“We could just keep going till Kanyakumari,” Shah said. “It’s like why would we ever stop?” {085-S03} Ten to thirty kilometres a day would get them there.

Amit Varma, who does not go on hikes, declined to say a word about it. But he recalled the day before the shoot, when Shah was asked whom he would take on a last hike. Shah’s answer, “Amit, will you come?”, made everyone tear up a bit. {085-S04}
third.caption: the walk that need not end

p2.title: Three little words
p2.deck: How Amit Varma and Ajay Shah sorted the world into three verdicts, and where they fell out

sections.label: Cities and curiosity
sections.head: Rabbit holes welcome
sections.caption: why people are brains, not stomachs
body: The opening verdicts were unanimous. Cities, Amit Varma said, bring diverse people together, which enlarges your worldview and your exposure to art, culture and ideas. Larger economic networks let people specialise. People crib about traffic, but they keep moving to cities. “They vote with their feet.” {085-C01}
Ajay Shah said villages are a hotbed of ignorance and unfreedom, and Varma recalled B.R. Ambedkar’s phrase, “dens of ignorance and vice”.

Curiosity got the same grade. A friend complained to Varma that he had spent three hours in a rabbit hole that had nothing to do with his life. Varma’s reply: “Fantastic. That’s what you should do.” {#rabbithole}
## Know thyself

Evolution, Shah said, applies far beyond biology: to jihadist groups in Iraq, to business models, to computer software. Varma added that you can only know yourself through evolutionary biology and psychology, because we are not blank slates. But an ought does not follow from an is, and our instincts often contradict each other. {085-C03}
Varma recommended Steven Pinker’s *The Blank Slate*, and said, admitting the hyperbole, that he divides his life into before and after reading it. {085-R05}

~ The humanities were underrated too, though Varma had nothing but contempt for humanities departments. {085-C13} Shah explained STEM’s prestige: it is easy to teach and to test. Prove Pythagoras’ theorem in an exam hall, and you can be thrown Apollonius’ theorem next.

quote.text: We paint a picture of the world by joining dots. The more dots we have, the more high definition our picture.

sections.label: Luck and failure
sections.head: Moonshots or lucky dice?
sections.caption: Elon Musk and survivorship bias
body: Elon Musk produced the second disagreement of the day. Ajay Shah said there is a large element of luck in the making of every rich person, after which great man syndrome leads them to opine on everything. He recommended the hosts’ own episode *A Country Is Not a Company* to Mr Musk. {085-R09}
Amit Varma called Musk a pioneering thinker, whose bets on electric cars, batteries and space went against conventional thinking.
Shah replied that a rough idea that the RBI needs reform is very different from actually doing it. {085-C06}
Few people even attempt such audacious bets, Varma countered, and even if only one in a hundred survives, “we need all those hundred”. {#audacious}
## Wish them failure
Failure, Varma said, is underrated. Anything good in him comes from having failed all his life, which stripped away his hubris and entitlement and turned him from a whiner into a doer. {085-C07}
Shah added that mass culture worships billionaires, and recalled an old Marwari culture in which a man’s worth is measured by the number of failed businesses he has run.
~ Talent, by contrast, was overrated. Varma recalled an athlete’s definition of it: going running at 5 am, hungover, with a cold and the next event six months away, in the rain. {085-S10}

quote.text: The best thing I can wish for for a young person is I wish you failure.

sections.label: The big fight
sections.head: Flat earth, open minds
sections.caption: heretics and reverence for knowledge
body: Flat-earth theory, both hosts agreed, is complete nonsense. What follows from that was their sharpest disagreement. {#hogwash}

Amit Varma still found something to defend. Heliocentrism was once heresy, he said, and so was questioning the consensus that sugar is fine and fat is the problem. American guidelines enshrined that consensus in 1977, and the obesity epidemic began. {#sugar}
Gregor Mendel, a complete outsider, was recognised only after his death; Ignaz Semmelweis was ignored for decades. Thinking heretical thoughts, Varma argued, is how humanity progresses.
## Who gets a say

Ajay Shah was “a little more status quo”. Experts define what is open for debate: intermittent fasting is, a flat earth is not. A teenager deciding on Reddit whether a COVID vaccine works, he said, is the modern post-truth world.
“The crisis of the modern world is an assault on knowledge,” Shah said. {085-C08}
They partly converged. An ordinary person, Varma conceded, can default to the conventional view, while a heretic should put their ideas out there.

~ On social media they parted again. Shah thinks it a net negative. Varma accepts Jonathan Haidt’s research on teenage girls, but said a curated feed lets you hear “the best minds in the world thinking aloud every day”. {085-C17}

quote.text: It is important to think heretical thoughts for humanity to progress.

sections.label: Less is freer
sections.head: Own less, gossip less
sections.caption: why frugality buys freedom
body: Ajay Shah opened with a borrowed line: “Freedom’s just another word for nothing left to lose.” The lower your fixed commitments, he said, the freer you are. {085-C10}

Amit Varma agreed that clearing out the inessential frees space in your head. He could live out of a suitcase, he said, because the real value is in the cloud and in his relationships. But he would not be dogmatic: books, good food and comfortable travel are fine if you can afford them. Just don’t buy private jets.
Shah, for his part, marvelled at the miracles they take for granted. His XKDR Forum rents a GPU for eight dollars an hour, a capability he called unimaginable. {085-C16}
## Mind your hours
Gossip, Varma said, is the most toxic thing in the world. “I would never speak bad things about any of you behind your back, but I have to your face very often.” {085-J06}
Shah’s friend Josh Felman, an older figure who commanded respect, had a cure. Whenever talk turned to who was sleeping with whom, he would put his hands down and say, “It’s not important.” {085-S02}
~ Little minds discuss people, medium minds discuss news, great minds discuss ideas, Shah said. Watch your hours: the rest is petty bickering. {085-J28}

quote.text: The lower the operational leverage of your life, the more you get freedom. So frugality buys you freedom. The price of freedom is frugality.

sections.label: Love and kin
sections.head: Unbundling the marriage
sections.caption: marriage as a bundled package
body: Marriage, both hosts said, is complicated. Amit Varma credited Ajay Shah with the frame: marriage is a package of love, sex, romance, companionship, parenthood and friendship. Few people unbundle it in their heads, so when one part falls apart, everything seems to. {085-C15}

Shah called it an institution of the agricultural world of religion and patriarchy, out of touch with a post-industrial age that is closer to the hunter-gatherer one. The 20th century, he added, put an excessive burden on one person to be your everything.

Varma said both of them were taking a privileged male view. For most women in India, he said, marriage is closer to imprisonment. Chinmay Tumbe’s *India Moving* shows that most internal migration in India happens when women marry and move to their husband’s place. {085-R14}
## The consent argument

Varma once wrote a tongue-in-cheek column arguing that having children is immoral: a child cannot consent to being born, will feel pain and will die. Then he shrugged. We do many sinful things, he said, like the white lies that sustain friendships, so go ahead. {085-C12}
~ Shah rated parenthood underrated. Parent-child journeys are among the great ones, he said, once you strip away resource-intensive, helicopter, performative and competitive parenting.

quote.text: I only wish it had been us, but I’m happy for your happiness.
quote.who: Warren Zevon, as quoted by Amit Varma

side.boxTitle: The first name on the list
side.boxText: Frédéric Bastiat was the first name the crew threw, and Amit Varma rated him underrated: a writer who put complex ideas simply without dumbing them down. His essay *That Which Is Seen and That Which Is Not Seen* named Varma’s podcast. {085-R02}

contQuote.text: Happiness is not something you experience, it is something you remember. As the years go by and as I have become older, life is actually a collection of peak experiences.

p3.title: Stories between verdicts
p3.deck: Four tales the hosts told along the way

stories.start: So I played this interesting form of poker once called match poker
stories.end: it simply won't work and it was a nightmare. But we were Asian champions
stories.caption: playing poker for India
stories.kicker: Amit Varma, out of retirement, on a game with new rules
stories.head: First principles, first in Asia
body: Playing for the country was one of the words thrown at the hosts. Ajay Shah rated it overrated. Amit Varma called it complicated, and declared an interest: he has played for India.
Varma was a professional poker player for five years, until 2015. Then a friend who owned the Haryana Hawks, a team in an IPL-style league, brought him out of retirement.

The game was match poker, which changes the rules so that the usual heuristics no longer apply. You had to think from first principles and sort out the new game. “And I did, and no one else did,” Varma said. {085-S09}
The Hawks won twice. Then Varma played for India, and the team won the Asian championship.
At the world championship in Greece, India got slaughtered. Three teammates could not get visas, and the replacements had to be taught a shared strategy on the fly. It was, Varma said, a nightmare.
He had a similar run in chess variants on chess.com, Atomic and Fog of War, where he was briefly number one until he got bored. The joy, he said, was in figuring out first principles.
His defence of playing for the country, partly tongue in cheek, was narrow: in some sports, such as Olympic events, the national team is the only stage there is.
~ Shah had made his own case first. Gukesh won the world championship in chess, he said. “You didn’t, I didn’t.” {085-C22}
stories.why: When a game is new, inherited heuristics stop working and whoever reasons from first principles takes the edge. Varma did it twice, in match poker and in chess variants on chess.com. {085-S09}
stories.postscript: Varma recommends the show’s poker episode for more on his five years as a professional.

stories.start: When I was young, I loved comics, but it was the early 1980s
stories.end: early game of poker in this versus a good memory around my dad
stories.caption: his father’s comics ration
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a father, a son and a supply of Marvel
stories.head: A ration of Marvel
body: In early-1980s Chandigarh, Amit Varma recalled, foreign comics were nearly impossible to find beyond the likes of Phantom and Indrajal. His father found a supplier in Delhi and brought back Marvel and DC comics from his trips.
He handed them over three at a time, and said three was all he had. When Varma got really bored, three more appeared.

Varma knew there were more. “So now game theory comes into play,” he said. {085-S05} He schemed to get them sooner, his father figured out he was playing the game, and it became an early game of poker.

~ Through those comics he fell for the Marvel universe of Stan Lee and his collaborators, whose characters were shades of grey. The Marvel Cinematic Universe, he said, is a cynical commercial exploitation of the franchise.
stories.why: Varma calls it a good memory of his father: two people playing game theory with each other, each knowing the other knew. It also explains his split verdict on Marvel, underrated on the page and overrated on screen.
stories.postscript: Shah asked whether the films could be made by an LLM. Varma: “Iron Man 38 can of course be made by LLM.” {085-J10}

stories.start: I was recording an episode of The Scene in the Unseen with a friend
stories.end: actually on the show. But I love the guy for it
stories.caption: a friend’s rant about sameness
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on an observation made over tea
stories.head: A scandal of sameness
body: Over tea, while recording an episode of *The Seen and the Unseen*, a friend of Amit Varma’s, “a distinguished gentleman who also happens to be gay”, said that two young celebrities had done Botox. One of them was about 20.
Varma was shocked. That was nothing, the friend said: they had boob jobs too.

Then he leaned forward. “Amit, I want you to go out there and I want you to look at the breasts of young women today. Look closely. They are all the same.” In his time, he said, there was variety and diversity. It was a scandal. {085-S08}

~ Varma says he did not follow the instructions. His own stance is to be comfortable in your own body, with exceptions for health and for repair after accidents, and to treat anyone who judges your looks as toxic.
stories.why: Behind the delightful rant was a real point: cosmetic procedures sand away human variety. Ajay Shah linked it to fashion. These are superficial props, he said, and the lifelong journey is one of building character.
stories.postscript: Shah’s soundtrack: the Eagles, whose high-livers “took all the right pills”. {085-J27}

stories.start: I like cooking once in a while, especially when I'm on my special diet
stories.end: happened to be good. Though you said it about Elon Musk, I don't
stories.caption: the best prawns he ever ate
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a happy accident in his kitchen
stories.head: Fluke in the frying pan
body: Amit Varma once ate one meal a day, between five and seven in the evening, and was ten kilos lighter. He cooked three-course meals for himself.
One day he marinated prawns in gochugaru, a Korean spice, with olive oil and gin, then cooked them in olive oil with lots of butter and bird’s-eye chilli.
His mind was blown for two reasons. “One reason was that this is the best prawn I have ever eaten. And the second reason was I made it.” {085-S07}

~ He called it a happy accident, or “the Elon Musk of my food”: survivorship bias, one in a million that happened to be good. “Though you said it about Elon Musk,” he told Ajay Shah, “I don’t.” {085-J16}
stories.why: Culinary experimentation is underrated, Varma said. He hates pineapple on pizza but defends the right to try it, and likes chowmein dosa, because all food evolved from something else. Ajay Shah added that this is how we keep inventing stuff.

quiz.q: Which writer’s essay gave Amit Varma’s podcast, The Seen and the Unseen, its name?
quiz.a: Frédéric Bastiat, with *That Which Is Seen and That Which Is Not Seen*.

quiz.q: How many Elon Musks did Ajay Shah say are out there rolling the dice?
quiz.a: 16,384, and out of dumb luck we venerate one of them.

quiz.q: How did Amit Varma complete the party game “There are two kinds of people”?
quiz.a: The whiners and the doers: a vicious cycle against a virtuous one.

quiz.q: Where did Ajay Shah and Ayush Patnaik realise they could simply keep walking to?
quiz.a: All the way to Kanyakumari, from a north-south route in the Sahyadris.

quiz.q: What happens to Amit Varma’s chess.com rating when he is on modafinil or keto?
quiz.a: It goes up by about a hundred points, and drops back afterwards.

quiz.q: Why does Warsaw mean more to Ajay Shah than Prague does?
quiz.a: He has spent years reading about Poland, and knows little about Prague.
